CFBC · Pure Mathematics Unit 2 · Module 1, Chapter 3

Partial fractions,
un-added

Adding fractions is easy. This chapter is that same skill in reverse — taking one awkward fraction apart into the simple pieces it was built from. There are only two questions to ask and four shapes to recognise, and this page drills all of them.

Every idea, distilled

Fourteen cards in the same shape: what triggers it, the rule, how to think about it, one worked example, and the mistakes that cost marks.

Two gates first

Answer two questions before you write a single letter.

What you are actually doing

When you see: A single fraction with a factorised denominator

Adding fractions is easy; un-adding them is the hard direction. Partial fractions is that reverse gear. You take one awkward fraction and split it back into the simple pieces that were added together to make it.

Forwards (easy)
Backwards (this chapter)
How to think about it
  • Do the forward calculation once, by hand. Seeing turn into makes the reverse feel obvious instead of magical.
  • The sign matters. A partial fraction statement is an identity — true for every value of , not just a few. That is exactly why you are allowed to substitute whatever you like.
  • Nothing is ever lost or gained. If you add your answer back together you must recover the original fraction, every time.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Treating it as a new kind of algebra
It is the fraction addition you have done since first form, run backwards. Nothing new is being invented.

Connects to: Everything in this chapter, and Chapter 4 — integration uses this constantly.

Gate 1: is it proper?

When you see: Any rational fraction, before you do anything else

Compare the highest power on top with the highest power on the bottom. Top smaller means proper, and you may go straight on. Top the same or bigger means improper, and you must divide first — no exceptions.

Proper
Improper
Example
How to think about it
  • Expand the denominator in your head just far enough to see its degree. is degree ; is degree .
  • This is a ten-second check that saves an entire wasted page. Skipping it is the most expensive mistake in the chapter.
  • Equal degrees still count as improper. needs dividing, even though the powers match.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Splitting an improper fraction directly
Your identity will have no solution, or you will get nonsense constants. The degrees simply do not match up.
×  Forgetting that equal degrees are improper
'Proper' means strictly smaller on top.

Connects to: Sends you to Improper fractions if it fails. Otherwise straight on to Gate 2.

Gate 2: factorise the bottom

When you see: A proper fraction whose denominator is not yet fully factorised

You cannot split a fraction until you know what it is made of. Factorise the denominator completely — into linear factors and irreducible quadratics — before you set anything up.

Difference of squares
Common factor
Irreducible — leave it
Test for irreducible
How to think about it
  • Always check whether a quadratic factor actually factorises before treating it as a quadratic case. looks quadratic but is really two linear factors in disguise.
  • Use the discriminant. has , so it is genuinely irreducible and gets an on top.
  • A factor of on its own counts as a linear factor: . So is a repeated linear factor and a distinct one.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Treating as an irreducible quadratic
It factorises. You would set up and never finish.
×  Trying to factorise
It has no real roots. Leave it whole and give it a linear numerator.

Connects to: Decides which of the four shapes each factor belongs to.

The four shapes

Every denominator factor falls into one of four cases.

The one rule that generates all four cases

When you see: Any factorised denominator

You do not need to memorise four separate templates. Every case follows from one sentence: the numerator above a factor is always one degree lower than that factor. And a factor repeated times gets every power from up to .

Over a linear factor
Over a quadratic factor
Repeated factor
The counting check
How to think about it
  • The counting check is your safety net. Before solving anything, count your letters and compare with the degree of the denominator. If they disagree, your setup is wrong and no amount of algebra will save it.
  • has degree , so you need exactly three letters: , , . has degree , so you need five: , , , , .
  • A quadratic factor is worth two letters, because is two unknowns. That is why the counting works out.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Putting a single constant over a quadratic factor
is not general enough. A degree- factor needs a degree- numerator: .
×  Giving a repeated factor only its highest power
alone cannot work. You need .

Connects to: Every one of the four shapes below is this rule applied to a different kind of factor.

Shape 1: unrepeated linear factors

When you see: Distinct brackets like , each appearing once

The friendliest case. One constant on top of each bracket, and the zeros of those brackets hand you the constants almost for free.

Template
Letters needed
How to think about it
  • Substitute the value of that makes each bracket zero. Every other term dies and one letter drops out immediately.
  • It works for awkward brackets too: for , substitute .
  • With three or more factors the substitution method is far quicker than equating coefficients. Use it.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Forgetting to multiply every term by the full denominator
Each term loses only its own bracket — the others stay.
×  Substituting the wrong sign
gives , not .

Connects to: The base case. Shapes 2, 3 and 4 are all this plus one extra idea.

Shape 2: repeated linear factors

When you see: A bracket raised to a power, like or

A factor repeated times needs fractions — one for every power from to . Miss any of them and the identity cannot balance.

Template
In general
Letters needed
How to think about it
  • Substituting the repeated zero gives you the highest power's constant only. The others need a second idea — any other value of , or comparing coefficients.
  • counts as repeated twice plus once, so it needs three letters: .
  • A good order: substitute the zeros first to get what you can, then substitute (or compare the coefficient) to mop up the rest.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Writing only and stopping
The lower power is missing. You need both and .
×  Expecting the repeated zero to give you everything
It gives you one constant. The rest need another substitution.

Connects to: Combines with Shape 1 in almost every exam question.

Shape 3: unrepeated quadratic factors

When you see: An irreducible quadratic like , ,

A quadratic factor that will not break down gets a linear numerator, . That is the one rule again: one degree below the factor.

Template
Letters needed
How to think about it
  • Check it really is irreducible first. If it factorises and belongs in Shape 1 or 2 instead.
  • You can still substitute the linear factor's zero to get instantly. The quadratic has no real zero to substitute, so and come from comparing coefficients or from convenient values like .
  • Comparing the highest power and the constant term usually gives you two quick equations.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Writing
Not general enough — a quadratic denominator needs on top.
×  Not checking the discriminant
If the quadratic factorises, this whole setup is the wrong shape.

Connects to: The same idea extends to Shape 4, where the quadratic is repeated.

Shape 4: repeated quadratic factors

When you see: An irreducible quadratic raised to a power, like

Both extra ideas at once: a linear numerator because the factor is quadratic, and every power from to because it is repeated. This is the longest case, but no new thinking is required.

Template
Letters needed
How to think about it
  • Expect four or five letters and a longer solve. That is normal for this case — it is not a sign you have gone wrong.
  • Substitute the zero of any linear factor first for a free constant, then equate coefficients of the highest power and work downwards.
  • The counting check earns its keep here. is degree , so exactly five letters: .
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Using
Two letters where four are needed. The counting check catches this instantly.
×  Panicking at the length
It is Shape 2 and Shape 3 stacked. Same method, more bookkeeping.

Connects to: The hardest shape, and the rarest. If you can set it up, you can set up anything.

Finding the letters

Three ways to pin down the constants — and when each is fastest.

Method 1: substitute the zeros

When you see: Any linear factor in the denominator

Because the statement is an identity, it holds for every — so you get to choose values that make life easy. Choose the ones that make brackets vanish.

Clear the fractions first
Then choose $x$
Example
How to think about it
  • This is the fastest method whenever the denominator is all linear factors. One substitution, one constant, no simultaneous equations.
  • Do not stop at the zeros. Once they are used up, any convenient value — usually — gives you another equation.
  • Fractional zeros are fine. Substituting is less work than solving two simultaneous equations.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Only substituting whole numbers
You lose the shortcut. The zero of is , and it is still the fastest substitution available.

Connects to: Pairs with equating coefficients when substitution runs out of useful values.

Method 2: the cover-up shortcut

When you see: Distinct linear factors only — and you want the answer in seconds

A one-line trick for unrepeated linear factors. Cover a bracket with your finger, put its zero into everything you can still see, and what you get is that bracket's constant.

The move
Example
How to think about it
  • It is Method 1 with the writing removed — same mathematics, no working. Use it to check answers even when you must show full working for the marks.
  • It only works on unrepeated linear factors. For a repeated factor it gives you the highest power's constant and nothing else.
  • Two brackets, two covers, done. On a multiple-choice question this takes about ten seconds.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Using cover-up on a quadratic factor
There is no real zero to substitute. It does not apply.
×  Using it on and expecting both constants
You get the one sitting over . The other still needs work.

Connects to: A fast version of Method 1. Perfect for checking a long answer.

Method 3: equating coefficients

When you see: Quadratic factors, repeated factors, or anything substitution cannot finish

Expand both sides, then match the coefficient of each power of . Two identical polynomials must agree term by term, which turns the identity into a set of simultaneous equations.

The principle
Where to start
How to think about it
  • Start at the ends. The highest power and the constant term normally involve only one or two letters each.
  • You rarely need this method alone. The efficient route is: substitute every zero you can, then use one or two coefficient comparisons to finish.
  • Comparing the constant term is the same as substituting . Use whichever you find easier to see.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Comparing coefficients before expanding fully
Every bracket must be multiplied out first, or terms get missed.
×  Using it when substitution would do
For three distinct linear factors, three substitutions beat three simultaneous equations every time.

Connects to: The only method that always works. Slowest, but it never fails you.

Finishing

Improper fractions, checking, and what this is really for.

Improper fractions: divide first

When you see: Gate 1 failed — the top degree is greater than or equal to the bottom

You cannot split an improper fraction. Divide it first: the answer becomes a polynomial plus a proper remainder fraction, and only that remainder gets decomposed.

The shape of the answer
Then split the remainder
How to think about it
  • Long division, or rewrite the numerator cleverly. For the bottom expands to , so the quotient is just .
  • The polynomial part never gets split. It is already as simple as it can be.
  • Check the degrees again after dividing. The remainder must now be strictly lower than the denominator, or you have not divided far enough.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Splitting without dividing
The algebra will not close. There is no choice of constants that works.
×  Dropping the quotient at the end
The polynomial part is part of the answer. Write it down.

Connects to: Sends the leftover proper fraction back through the four shapes.

Checking without redoing it

When you see: You have an answer and two minutes left

Three checks, each faster than reworking the question. Any one of them will catch most errors.

Count
Substitute
Cover-up
How to think about it
  • The substitution check is the strongest. Pick any that does not make a denominator zero — usually — and evaluate both sides.
  • If your answer's denominators are not exactly the factors you started with, stop. Something has gone wrong in the setup, not the arithmetic.
  • Signs are where marks go. A negative constant is completely normal; a negative that should be positive is not.
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Assuming it is right because the algebra felt smooth
One substitution takes fifteen seconds and settles it.

Connects to: Applies to every shape in the chapter.

Why you are learning this

When you see: Chapter 4, and beyond

Partial fractions is not really a topic — it is a tool you are being handed early so that the next chapter is possible. On its own it is a party trick; attached to integration it is essential.

Impossible as it stands
Routine once split
Also used for
How to think about it
  • Every integrates to a logarithm. That is the whole reason the chapter exists.
  • When you meet an integral with a factorised quadratic or cubic on the bottom, your first thought should be partial fractions.
  • The repeated-factor terms integrate to powers, not logs: gives .
Worked in one breath
Where it goes wrong
×  Learning the mechanics without the purpose
You will meet this again within a fortnight, inside an integral. Recognising it there is the real assessment.

Connects to: Chapter 4: Integration — where this becomes a weekly habit.

Warm-up

The denominator is not ready to use yet. Everything depends on spotting that before you write a single letter.

Step 1. What is the first move?

How to study this

Learning it, and keeping it

Eight habits that make this topic almost mechanical. None of them involve rereading the notes.

Run the two gates every single time

Is it proper? Is the bottom fully factorised? Those two questions take ten seconds and decide the entire question. Almost every zero-mark answer in this topic comes from skipping one of them and confidently solving the wrong problem.

Try this: Write 'proper?' and 'factorised?' at the top of your rough working before you start. Every time, until you stop needing to.

Count your letters before you solve

The number of unknown constants equals the degree of the denominator. Always. Count them the moment you write the setup down — if they disagree, stop and rebuild rather than pressing on.

Try this: Cover the answers in Drill 2 above and do all ten in under two minutes. That is the whole skill.

One rule, not four templates

The numerator above any factor is one degree lower than that factor, and a factor repeated times gets every power up to . Those two sentences generate all four cases, so there is nothing else to memorise.

Try this: Take any denominator from the exercise set and write only the skeleton — no constants found, no working. Ten of them takes five minutes and trains the part that is actually tested.

Substitute zeros first, coefficients second

Substituting the zero of a bracket kills every other term at once. Use up all of them before touching simultaneous equations — it is faster and there is far less to get wrong.

Try this: When you get stuck for a last constant, try before you try anything clever.

Learn cover-up as a checking tool

Even when the marks require full working, cover-up lets you verify each constant in seconds. Write the full method for the examiner, then check yourself with cover-up before moving on.

Try this: Redo any past-paper distinct-linear question by cover-up alone. If your two answers disagree, you have found a mistake for free.

Do it backwards to check

Adding your partial fractions back together must return the original. You do not have to do the whole addition — substituting one value of into both sides is enough to catch a wrong constant.

Try this: Use unless it makes a denominator zero. Then use .

Expect the ugly answers

Constants of , or are completely normal here. A messy fraction is not evidence that you went wrong, and chasing 'nicer' numbers leads people to invent errors.

Try this: When an answer looks ugly, check it by substitution rather than by feel.

Remember where it is going

You are being taught this so that next chapter you can integrate things that are otherwise impossible. Every time you split a fraction, notice that each piece is something you already know how to integrate.

Try this: After each practice question, ask: what would the integral of my answer be? It takes ten seconds and doubles what the question teaches you.
